second_read.design: Customer-week panel (170 weeks, Jan 2008-Mar 2011) of a wine-and-spirits retailer's loyalty-card customers; treatment = the customer joining the firm's social media page and thereby receiving firm-generated content, with join dates staggered across 412 treated customers (Figure 2); comparison = 412 never-participating customers selected by 1:1 nearest-neighbor propensity-score matching.
second_read.reason: The FGC_iht indicator switches on at each treated customer's own join date (footnote 6, Figure 2), so the design is staggered and binary with never-treated controls. But every main-text specification violates the rules: the control group is constructed by propensity-score matching (matching-based DiD); the DID model in Equations 1-4 and Table 3 (M1-M5) has pair-level intercepts a0ih but no calendar-week fixed effects, and M2-M5 add time-varying controls (TVAd, Email, CExp, PromD/CrossP), triple interactions with customer characteristics, AR(1) errors, and a Type I Tobit (nonlinear) in M5, all estimated by hierarchical Bayes MCMC; Table 5 repeats this for profit. Treatment is customer self-selection into the firm's page rather than an externally timed rollout. design: 830 B2B customers whose sales rep voluntarily left a U.S. electrical-components distributor at rep-specific dates during 2011 (treated) vs. 1,615 stratified-random customers whose rep stayed (never treated); outcome is log customer sales collapsed into one year before (T1) and one year after (T2) each departure date.
reason: Departure dates differ across quarters of 2011, so adoption is staggered and binary with a never-treated comparison group. But every main-text specification (Table 7 Columns 1-5, Tables 10-11) collapses each treated customer into pre/post windows aligned on its own departure date. These models use a treatment-group dummy, a relative Post_Period dummy, and departure-quarter dummies, not calendar-time fixed effects, so they amount to an event-aligned, stacked-style 2x2. Columns 2-5 add random customer effects, branch and industry dummies, and predetermined covariates, and Column 5 adds a Heckman inverse Mills ratio; Table 9 uses propensity-score and Mahalanobis matching.
appendix_only_specs: Web Appendix reports a two-quarter window DiD (-.432) and matching (-.376), sales-volatility and peer-dissimilarity robustness checks, and matching by replacement type; all use the same event-aligned two-period design.
notes: Closest to eligible is Table 7 Column 1 (OLS: treatment dummy, relative post dummy, interaction -.193 (.053), departure-quarter FE, no covariates), but its time dimension is event time, not calendar time. The paper does not say how control customers' T1/T2 windows are dated. A calendar-quarter panel with unit and quarter FE could in principle be built from the underlying transactions, but the article does not report one. Tables 10-11 split treatment by new-hire vs existing-rep replacement and interact DD with continuous similarity and performance measures.
data_statement: Proprietary customer transaction and HR data from an unnamed Fortune 500 U.S. distributor of electrical components; no data or code availability statement (an online supplement at the JM DOI holds web appendices only).

second_read.design: Customers of a U.S. B2B electrical-components distributor; treatment = the customer's sales rep departs (voluntary turnover) and the account is reassigned, at rep-specific departure dates spread across 2011 (129 reps); 830 treated customers versus 1,615 stratified-random control customers whose reps never departed; outcome is log annual sales one year before versus one year after the departure date.
second_read.reason: Underlying adoption is staggered and binary with never-treated controls, but the article collapses the panel into two event-time periods (T1 = year before, T2 = year after the departure date) and estimates Eq. 1-5 as 2x2 DiD regressions with a treatment-group dummy, a relative-time Post dummy, and their interaction, using customer random effects rather than unit fixed effects and departure-quarter dummies rather than calendar-time fixed effects. Table 7 Column 1 (coef -.193, SE .053) is the only controls-free column but it is this two-period event-time collapse without unit or calendar-time FE; Columns 2-5 add time-varying customer and rep covariates, branch and industry FE, and a Heckman inverse Mills ratio. Tables 9 (matching), 10, 11 (ten-quarter window) and 12 share these features.
second_read.appendix_only_specs: Web Appendix: two-quarter window versions of the DiD and PSM estimates, subsample matching results for new-hire vs existing-rep reassignments, robustness with sales volatility and peer-dissimilarity controls, lagged unemployment instruments. All appear to use the same two-period collapse.
second_read.notes: The authors explicitly cite Bertrand, Duflo, and Mullainathan (2004) as the reason for collapsing to two periods. A replicator could in principle rebuild a customer-quarter staggered panel from the 2008-2013 transaction data, but no such specification is reported. Verdict could be read as ineligible if the lead requires a calendar-time panel regression to appear in the article; I classify it as near-miss because the adoption design itself is staggered and binary and 'two-period collapse' is a listed near-miss reason. Treatment never switches off.
